title: Serialisation, JSON and the danger of unsafe deserialisation

videos.script: A program's objects live in its memory, and they die with it. To keep them, or to send them to another program, they have to become bytes, and then become objects again on the other side. {{java}} Java has its own way to do that, built in since the nineties. It is two lines of code, and the bytes it writes name the classes they should become. {{danger}} That is the problem. A program that reads those bytes from outside lets whoever wrote them choose what it builds. The defence is a filter that allows a short list of classes and refuses everything else, before a single object is made. {{json}} Then the format most programs actually exchange: JSON. A small Maven project, one library, and a record turned into text and back. {{input}} And last, JSON that arrives from outside: an extra field, a missing one, a number spelled out in words, and what the library does with each.
